title: Learning versus replying
objectives: Separate training, inference, and saved conversation state.
Learn a simple next-word preference by counting examples.
prediction: Your toy sees 'cats eat fish' twice and 'cats eat rice' once. Which word should a most-common-word rule select after eat? Decide before running the code.
explanation: Training is the stage where examples change a model's learned parameters. Inference is using those learned parameters to produce an output. Think of learning recipes versus cooking one meal with a recipe you already know.
Our toy learns counts. Every training sentence contributes an observation: what word followed eat? Two fish observations and one rice observation make fish the most common in this small dataset.

collections.Counter is a Python dictionary-like counter. Counter(['fish', 'fish', 'rice']) records how many times each item occurs. most_common(1) asks for the single most frequent item and its count.

A saved chat is different again. The application stores messages and can supply them as context on a later request. Saving a message or changing a prompt does not, by itself, retrain the hosted model.
analogy_limit: Recipe learning is an analogy. Our count table has no neural weights, gradient optimization, or transformer layers. Real LLM training is far more complex than counting a few words.

python_example.code:
from collections import Counter

training_sentences = ['cats eat fish', 'dogs eat fish', 'birds eat rice']
following_eat = Counter()
for sentence in training_sentences:
    words = sentence.split()
    if words[1] == 'eat':
        following_eat[words[2]] += 1
print(dict(following_eat))
prediction = following_eat.most_common(1)[0][0]
print(prediction)
walkthrough: split() creates a list of words. This dataset always has three words, so its fixed indexes are safe only for these examples.
The loop learns counts from the training sentences.
most_common(1) returns a list containing a (word, count) pair. The first [0] selects that pair; the second selects its word.
Selecting fish uses the counts; it does not add another observation.

game.title: Training or Playing?
game.instructions: Sort each action into training, inference, or app memory. Two of three correct passes.

rounds.prompt: You scan three example sentences and update the word counts.

feedback.a: The examples changed the toy's learned counts.
feedback.b: Here the stored counts change, so this is the learning stage.
feedback.c: You are fitting counts from examples, not storing a conversation record.

rounds.prompt: You use the existing count table to select fish.

feedback.b: You are using what the toy already learned.
feedback.c: No backup was created by selecting a word.

rounds.prompt: Your app saves 'My name is Mira' to SQLite for later context.

choices.text: The model gained a new neural layer

feedback.a: Saving chat history does not update the hosted model's parameters.
feedback.b: A database write does not alter model architecture.
feedback.c: The app can later send this message as context; that is separate from training.

questions.prompt: What made fish the toy's preferred prediction?

choices.text: Fish appeared most often after eat in the examples
Fish is universally the correct food

feedback.a: The preference came from this dataset's counts.
feedback.b: The data does not prove a universal fact about animals.
feedback.c: The code counts observations; word length does not choose the result.

questions.prompt: Which action would change this toy's learned preference toward rice?

choices.text: Add enough rice training examples and rebuild counts

feedback.a: Printing does not feed observations back into this toy.
feedback.b: Changing training data and recomputing counts changes the learned preference.
feedback.c: A variable name does not change the counts.

questions.prompt: A hosted chatbot uses your name from a previous message. What might explain it?

choices.text: The app included that message in the request context
It must have read your computer files
Every reply permanently retrains the model

feedback.a: Normal chat generation does not imply retraining.
feedback.b: Name recall alone is not evidence of file access.
feedback.c: Conversation context can supply the name without updating the model.

build.title: Change what the toy learns
build.instructions: Add two more three-word training sentences ending in rice. Rebuild the counts and predict again. Before running it, calculate the new fish and rice counts yourself.
criteria: The new counts contain fish: 2 and rice: 3.
The new most-common prediction is rice, and you can explain why.
hints: For example, 'robots eat rice' has the required three-word shape.
Run the counting loop from an empty Counter after changing the dataset.
build.reference_solution:
from collections import Counter
sentences = ['cats eat fish', 'dogs eat fish', 'birds eat rice', 'robots eat rice', 'mice eat rice']
counts = Counter(sentence.split()[2] for sentence in sentences)
print(dict(counts))
print(counts.most_common(1)[0][0])

reflection: Describe one example each of training, inference, and application memory using your chatbot project.
tutor_context: Teach training versus inference versus app memory. Explain Counter and nested indexes with tiny lists. Count-table learning is a toy, not neural training.
